rationale: Z65, from the incoming-edge audit. A zig relationship carries six keys and BOTH endpoints are name strings; src/lsp/impact.ts obtains inbound edges by scanning outgoing edges and matching targets, so an edge's name is all a reverse walk has. Measured over the whole 3,834-file zig corpus through production parseFile (draw sha256:2f3545f9..., 392,550 edges): 265,887 edges (67.73%) name a target 2+ published symbols share, and 151,004 of those (56.79%) have a candidate in the edge's OWN file. This fixture pins the annotation that makes the second group resolvable without a cross-file guess, and pins the two cases where no per-file rule may be applied at all. Every row is a place where a plausible implementation would guess: the file-local kind, the in-file name collision, the external name, and the import path. The forbid rows are the ones that matter most, because the failure mode is a confident wrong answer rather than a missing one. Z66 amendment: the `ArrayList` rows changed SPELLING, not verdict — the same text is still external, and `meta.targetScope` is still `file-external`. What changed is that the edge now carries the receiver (`std.ArrayList`), so the two forbid rows pin the old leaf.

a call to an in-file method. This is one of the 151,004 edges a per-file rule resolves soundly
a field read of an in-file member

THE COLLISION, and the strong form of the assertion. `Collide` is a struct at :19 AND a function at :21, so the edge resolves file-locally but its KIND is undecidable. `meta.targetKind: null` means this edge must NOT carry a targetKind AT ALL, so the row fails for any kind the implementation might emit — including a third the fixture never heard of. The two forbid rows below pin the two kinds a plausible implementation would actually reach for, because `meta.x: null` in a FORBID has the opposite polarity: it forbids the ABSENCE of the key, which is why this assertion lives here and not there.

nothing in this file declares ArrayList, and the edge still SAYS the target is not a per-file binding (`meta.targetScope: file-external`) and still names the receiver (`std.ArrayList`) with its module. The `zigExternalRef` claim is correctly absent: it means "the target's OWNER is not published", and this target's owner is `std` — the file's own `const std = @import("std")`, which Z35 publishes as a constant. THE MARKER IS CORRECTLY ABSENT, and that is the point of this row (measured 2026-10-10, `validation/m14/fixtures/zig/external-claim-audit.ts` on the gate's 60-file stride): the arbiter reads `zigExternalRef` as an OWNER claim and verifies it by looking the owner up, and this target's owner IS the alias the source wrote (`std.ArrayList` -> owner `std`). Z35 publishes `const std = @import("std")` as a `constant` named `std`, so the claim was refuted on every one of the 259 such edges in the run and satisfied nothing. What the row still pins is the RECEIVER: the target is the qualified path and `zigImportAlias`/`zigImportModule` name the module, so a consumer can still exclude the edge by rule. The deep-path rows (`std.debug.assert`, `std.io.getStdOut`, `g.Object.new`) keep `zigExternalRef: true`, so a rule that dropped the key EVERYWHERE fails this fixture.
an import PATH. It can never be a symbol, so it is external by construction
containment is the strongest local case: the owner and the member are in one file by construction

The row mutant M5 exists to kill, and the row whose ABSENCE let it survive the first run. `const std = @import("std")` publishes a `std` constant in this file, so an edge naming `std` IS file-local. A forbid row alone was not enough: the mutant flips std to `file-external`, which SATISFIES a forbid that says std must not be external while satisfying nothing that says it must be local. A negative assertion with no positive counterpart is satisfied by any behaviour, which is what a surviving mutant looks like from the fixture side.

forbidRelationships.note: the in-file name collision must NOT be resolved to one kind. `Collide` names a struct at :19 and a function at :21; publishing either is a guess, and a confident guess is the expensive failure
the other half of the same collision — a forbid per candidate kind, because one forbid cannot fail for both

THE PRE-Z66 SPELLING. `std.ArrayList(u8)` is a generic type application and the analyzer used to publish its leaf alone, which is indistinguishable from a call to a local `ArrayList`. A regression to the leaf would still satisfy every positive row above except this one, so the negative row is what makes the fixture falsifiable against it.
the declared-type twin of the same read. The declared-type pass qualifies through the same alias map, and a regression that fixed only the `calls` site would leave this row passing.
